stimuli.title: Rooftop hives
stimuli.text:
When a downtown hotel installed four beehives on its roof in 2009, the guests who noticed them mostly assumed the hives were a publicity stunt. Fifteen years later, rooftop beekeeping has spread to office towers, schools and apartment blocks in dozens of cities, and the stunt has become a small industry. Its supporters describe the hives as a lifeline for struggling pollinators.

The picture is more complicated than that. The honeybee is a managed, domesticated insect, and it is not in danger of disappearing; the bees whose numbers have fallen sharply are wild species, many of them solitary bees that nest in the ground or in hollow stems. Honeybees and wild bees feed on the same flowers. In a city, where flowering plants are scattered across parks, yards and planters, adding thousands of honeybees can leave less nectar and pollen for the wild bees that were already there. A study in one European capital found that wild bee visits to flowers dropped in neighborhoods where hive numbers had climbed fastest.

None of this means rooftop hives should be banned. They teach people about pollination, and the honey is a welcome local product. But a building owner who wants to help pollinators would often do more good by planting a roof garden of native flowers and leaving a few bare patches of soil than by bringing in another colony. The most useful question is not how many hives a city has, but how many flowers.

stimuli.title: Two views on homework in the early grades
stimuli.text:
**Passage 1**

Research on homework in the elementary grades has produced a remarkably consistent finding: for children under about ten, the amount of homework assigned has little measurable connection to how much they learn. What it does affect is family life. Nightly worksheets crowd out reading for pleasure, outdoor play and sleep, and they fall hardest on households where parents work evenings or cannot help with the material. Schools that have replaced assigned homework with a simple request that children read each night have generally reported no loss in achievement. Young children's evenings should belong to them.

**Passage 2**

It is true that a page of arithmetic at age seven does not raise test scores very much. But scores are not the only reason to assign homework. A short, regular task done at home teaches a child to remember materials, to manage a little time without an adult standing over them and to finish what was started. Those habits do not appear suddenly in middle school, when the workload grows; they have to be built. The real problem in many schools is not that homework exists but that it is too long and too dull. Ten focused minutes are worth more than an hour of busywork.

stimuli.title: Stranded boulders
stimuli.text: Scattered across the fields of New England are boulders that do not match the bedrock beneath them: a block of granite resting on limestone, say, many miles from the nearest granite outcrop. Early naturalists proposed floods to explain these wanderers, or erratics. The answer, accepted only in the mid-1800s, was ice. Continental glaciers had plucked the rocks from their sources, carried them for great distances and dropped them where the ice melted. Today geologists trace an erratic back to its parent outcrop to map the direction in which the ice once flowed.

stimuli.title: The card catalog
stimuli.text: For most of the twentieth century, finding a library book began at a wooden cabinet of small drawers. Each book had at least three cards, filed by author, by title and by subject, so a reader could approach it from any direction. The system depended on a standard card size, about three by five inches, which allowed libraries to buy ready-printed cards from a central supplier instead of writing their own. When online catalogs arrived in the 1980s and 1990s, they kept the same three access points; the drawers disappeared, but the logic of the cards survived on the screen.

stimuli.title: Glowing water
stimuli.text: On a moonless night in a few sheltered bays, every paddle stroke leaves a trail of blue-green light. The glow comes from dinoflagellates, single-celled organisms that flash when the water around them is disturbed. The bays where the effect is brightest share a narrow entrance that keeps the organisms from being flushed out to sea, along with mangroves whose fallen leaves supply nutrients. Visitors who expect to see it on any night are often disappointed, because the display depends on darkness, calm water and a healthy bay. On a good night, though, it is easily the most beautiful sight in the Caribbean.

stimuli.title: The lyceum movement
stimuli.text:
In 1826 a Massachusetts teacher named Josiah Holbrook proposed that towns form associations for mutual education, in which neighbors would meet through the winter to hear lectures and discuss them. He called the associations lyceums, after the school where Aristotle taught. Within a decade there were thousands of them, from New England villages to frontier towns in Ohio.

A lyceum evening was inexpensive and open to nearly anyone. A farmer might hear a talk on soil chemistry one week and on the history of Rome the next, and the speaker was as likely to be the local doctor as a visitor from the city. As railroads spread, however, the lyceum changed. Touring speakers could now reach dozens of towns in a single season, and organizers found that famous names filled halls. By the 1850s the most popular lecturers, among them writers and reformers, were paid handsome fees, and the program was set by a booking agent rather than by the members.

Historians disagree about whether this shift was a loss. Something was gained: audiences in small towns heard the leading thinkers of the age, and debates over abolition and women's rights reached people who would never have read the books. Yet the original idea, that ordinary people could teach one another, gave way to a model in which they mainly listened.

stimuli.title: Two views on daylight saving time
stimuli.text:
**Passage 1**

Each spring, moving the clocks forward an hour gives us long, bright evenings for the rest of the season. People use those evenings: retailers and sports leagues report more activity, and many people simply enjoy being outdoors after work. Supporters of a permanent switch argue that we should keep the later sunset all year and stop the twice-yearly disruption. Since the disruption itself is what most people complain about, ending the clock changes while keeping the brighter evenings seems an easy compromise.

**Passage 2**

The case against changing the clocks is strong, but the case for permanent daylight saving time is weak. Sleep researchers point out that our internal clocks are set mainly by morning light. Under permanent daylight saving time, winter sunrise in many northern cities would come after 8:30, and children would travel to school in the dark for months. The United States tried year-round daylight saving time in 1974 and abandoned it within a year after public opinion turned against the dark mornings. If the clocks are to stop changing, they should stay on standard time.

stimuli.title: Changing color
stimuli.text: An octopus can change the color of its skin in less than a second. The change is controlled by thousands of chromatophores, tiny sacs of pigment surrounded by muscles that stretch the sac open or squeeze it shut on a signal from the nervous system. Curiously, most octopuses appear to be color-blind: their eyes contain only one kind of light-sensitive pigment. How an animal that cannot see color matches its background so well remains an open question, though some researchers suspect the skin itself may sense light.

stimuli.title: Railroad time
stimuli.text: Before 1883 most American towns kept their own time, setting noon by the moment the sun stood highest overhead. Because the sun moves across the sky, noon in one town might be several minutes ahead of noon in a town to the west. For travelers on horseback the difference hardly mattered. For railroads, which ran many trains on shared tracks, it was dangerous, and timetables listed dozens of local times. In November 1883 the railroads adopted four standard time zones across the country. Congress did not make the zones law until 1918.

stimuli.title: Desire paths
stimuli.text: Walk through almost any park or campus and you will find narrow dirt trails worn across the grass where people have ignored the paved walkways. Planners call these desire paths. Some cities treat them as vandalism and put up fences. Others treat them as free information: a desire path shows exactly where people want to walk, and paving it often costs less than repairing the lawn year after year. A few universities have even waited a year after opening a new building before laying any walkways, so that students could show them where the paths belong.

stimuli.title: A vault for seeds
stimuli.text: Inside a mountain on a Norwegian island far above the Arctic Circle, a tunnel leads to three chambers kept at about minus 18 degrees Celsius. The chambers hold copies of seed samples from gene banks around the world. The vault is meant as a backup, not a first resort: each depositing bank keeps its own collection and can withdraw its samples if they are lost at home. That happened for the first time in 2015, when researchers whose gene bank in Syria had been damaged by war withdrew seeds to replant their collection in Lebanon and Morocco.

stimuli.title: Draft: the courtyard garden
stimuli.text:
(1) Three years ago, the courtyard behind Lincoln Middle School was a square of cracked asphalt that nobody used. (2) Today it is a garden with twelve raised beds, a compost bin and a rain barrel. (3) The change began with a science teacher, Ms. Ortiz, who asked her students to design a garden as a class project. (4) The students measured the space, researched which vegetables grow well in partial shade, and they wrote a budget. (5) The parent association liked the plan and paid for the lumber and soil.

(6) Now every grade uses the garden. (7) Sixth graders track how fast different seeds sprout. (8) Seventh graders test the soil. (9) Eighth graders sell the extra produce at a weekend market and keep the accounts. (10) The market is held in the school parking lot, which is also used for basketball. (11) Teachers say the garden has made abstract lessons real, and students who rarely spoke in class are often the ones explaining how the drip lines work.

stimuli.title: Draft: the tool library
stimuli.text:
(1) Most households own a power drill, but the average drill is used for only a few minutes in its entire life. (2) That fact inspired the Eastside Tool Library, which opened in a former bank branch last spring. (3) Members pay twenty dollars a year and can borrow anything on the shelves, from ladders to tile saws, for up to a week. (4) The idea is simple. (5) The work behind it is not.

(6) Volunteers check every tool when it comes back, sharpening blades and replacing worn cords. (7) They also teach short classes on basic repairs, since a borrowed tool is not much use to someone who has never held one. (8) Last year the library lent tools more than four thousand times. (9) Its organizers estimate that members saved over sixty thousand dollars by borrowing instead of buying. (10) They hope to open a second location, even though they have not yet found a building.

stimuli.title: Draft: night skies
stimuli.text: (1) For most of human history, anyone could look up on a clear night and see the band of the Milky Way. (2) Today, about a third of people on Earth cannot, because the glow of artificial light hides it. (3) Astronomers were the first to complain about this glow, which is called light pollution. (4) Biologists have since joined them. (5) Many birds migrate at night and use the stars to navigate, and bright cities can pull them off course. (6) Newly hatched sea turtles crawl toward the brightest horizon, which used to be the ocean. (7) Some towns have started to fight back. (8) They have replaced old streetlights with shielded fixtures that point light down at the road, where it is needed, instead of up at the sky.

questions.stem:
Students in Ms. Reyes's class who used a new reading app scored higher on the spring reading test than students who did not. The app's maker says this proves the app improves reading. Students chose for themselves whether to use the app.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the maker's conclusion?
options: Some students used the app at home as well as in school.
The students who chose the app were already stronger readers before the year began.
Ms. Reyes has taught reading for more than fifteen years.
The spring reading test was the same one given in earlier years.
The app costs less than most other reading programs that schools buy.
questions.explanation: If the app users were stronger readers from the start, their higher scores could reflect that head start rather than the app. Because students chose for themselves, this alternative explanation is likely.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is supported by the data in the table?
options: In-person visits fell in each year after 2020.
E-book loans fell in each year after reaching a peak in 2021.
E-book loans in 2023 were more than twice what they were in 2019.
In-person visits in 2023 were higher than in-person visits in 2019.
Program attendance rose every year from 2019 through 2023.
questions.explanation: E-book loans went from 95 thousand to 262 thousand, more than double. In-person visits in 2023 (690) were still below 2019 (820), program attendance fell in 2020, e-book loans kept rising after 2021, and visits rose after 2020.

questions.stem: In which year did program attendance first rise above its 2019 level?
options: It never rose above its 2019 level.
questions.explanation: Program attendance was 41 thousand in 2019. It fell to 12, 22 and 38 thousand in 2020 through 2022, then reached 47 thousand in 2023, the first year above 41.

questions.stem:
The town council voted to keep the public pool open until 9 p.m. on weeknights this summer, an hour later than last year. The decision followed a petition signed by more than six hundred residents, many of whom said that they could not reach the pool before it closed after work.

Which of the following can be inferred from the statement?
options: Many of the residents who signed the petition work until late afternoon or evening.
The council will keep the pool open until 9 p.m. in every future summer.
The pool was crowded during the day last summer because of the early closing.
Most of the town's residents signed the petition to keep the pool open later.
The pool cost the town less to operate last year than it will this year.
questions.explanation: The petitioners said they could not get to the pool before it closed after work, which implies that many of them work into the late afternoon or evening. Nothing supports claims about crowding, a majority of residents, future summers or costs.

questions.stem:
Some readers will find the new translation too free, since it often rearranges sentences and replaces old idioms with modern ones. I found it a revelation. For the first time, the characters sound like people talking rather than like a museum exhibit.

The author's attitude toward the new translation is best described as
options: enthusiastic approval
detached neutrality
cautious skepticism
mild disappointment
reluctant, grudging acceptance
questions.explanation: The author calls the translation "a revelation" and praises its natural dialogue. The author mentions other readers' objections only to set them aside.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Rooftop honeybees may compete with wild bees, so planting flowers is often a better way to help pollinators.
Cities should ban rooftop hives because they reduce the honey that wild bees are able to produce.
Rooftop beekeeping began as a hotel publicity stunt and has since grown into a profitable city industry.
Honeybees are disappearing from cities because rooftop hives do not supply them with enough flowers.
Building owners have learned that roof gardens of native flowers attract more guests than beehives do.
questions.explanation: The passage questions the claim that rooftop hives rescue pollinators: honeybees are not endangered, they compete with wild bees for flowers, and planting native flowers often helps more. The stunt history is only the opening, the passage rejects a ban, and wild bees do not make honey.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which bees have declined sharply in number?
options: Wild species, including many solitary bees
Bees that feed only on the flowers of parks
Domesticated honeybees kept in rooftop hives
Colonies moved from rural farms into cities
Honeybees living in large European capitals
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the honeybee "is not in danger of disappearing" and that "the bees whose numbers have fallen sharply are wild species, many of them solitary bees."

questions.stem: As used in the first paragraph, "stunt" most nearly means
options: a dangerous physical feat or trick
an act meant to attract attention
a trick performed by an animal
a scene filmed with a double
a check on growth or progress
questions.explanation: Guests assumed the hives were "a publicity stunt," something done to draw attention to the hotel. The other meanings of the word do not fit a hotel's hives.

questions.stem: The sentence "The picture is more complicated than that" at the start of the second paragraph serves mainly to
options: concede that the supporters' claim about pollinators is entirely correct
introduce a new example of a successful rooftop hive
summarize the history presented in the first paragraph
shift the topic from honeybees to the honey they produce
signal that the author will challenge the claim just described
questions.explanation: The first paragraph ends with supporters calling hives a lifeline for pollinators; the next sentence announces a complication, and the paragraph then explains why that claim is doubtful.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's argument that adding honeybee hives can harm wild bees in cities?
options: Honey from rooftop hives sells for a higher price than honey from rural farms.
Roof gardens of native flowers attract both honeybees and several different kinds of wild bees.
Most solitary bees nest in the ground or in hollow plant stems rather than in hives.
In cities where hive numbers rose sharply, wild bee visits to flowers stayed the same.
Some hotels added beehives to their roofs in order to attract guests' attention.
questions.explanation: The author's evidence is that wild bee visits dropped where hives multiplied. Finding no change in such cities would undercut the claim that honeybees crowd wild bees out. The other choices are consistent with the passage or irrelevant to it.

questions.stem:
Our town should build a second parking garage downtown. Shop owners say their customers complain about how hard it is to find a space, and more parking will bring more shoppers.

The argument assumes that
options: shoppers stay away from downtown mainly because parking is hard to find
shop owners know more about parking than town planners do
the town has enough money to build a second parking garage
the first parking garage downtown is too expensive to use
most shoppers would rather walk downtown than drive there
questions.explanation: The conclusion that more parking will bring more shoppers depends on the unstated idea that a lack of parking is what keeps shoppers away. If they stay away for other reasons, the garage would not help.

questions.stem:
Although the novel was dismissed by critics when it first appeared, it was never out of print, and a generation of readers who discovered it in used bookstores made it a classic.

Which of the following best restates the sentence?
options: Critics disliked the novel at first, but readers kept it alive and turned it into a classic.
The novel went out of print because critics dismissed it when it first appeared.
Critics praised the novel at first, and readers later found it in used bookstores.
A generation of critics discovered the novel and persuaded readers to buy it.
Used bookstores refused to sell the novel until critics changed their opinion of it.
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts the critics' early dismissal with readers who kept finding the book until it became a classic. It says the book was never out of print, so the claim that it went out of print contradicts it.

questions.skill: Main idea of a paired passage
questions.stem: The author of Passage 1 is primarily concerned with
options: arguing that homework for young children costs more than it delivers
explaining how parents can help children complete nightly worksheets
proving that schools without homework produce higher achievement
describing the habits that homework builds before middle school begins
showing that reading for pleasure raises test scores more than homework
questions.explanation: Passage 1 says homework for children under ten has little effect on learning but a real cost to family life, and concludes that "young children's evenings should belong to them." Schools that dropped homework reported "no loss," not a gain, so the claim that dropping homework produces higher achievement overstates it.

questions.stem: How would the author of Passage 2 most likely respond to the claim in Passage 1 that homework has little connection to how much young children learn?
options: By agreeing and recommending that homework be replaced with nightly reading
By granting that it is largely true but arguing that homework serves other purposes
By arguing that parents, not teachers, should decide how much homework to give
By rejecting it and citing studies showing large gains from early homework
By claiming that young children learn more from homework than from class time
questions.explanation: Passage 2 opens, "It is true that a page of arithmetic at age seven does not raise test scores very much," then argues that homework builds habits. It concedes the point rather than disputing it.

questions.stem: Both authors would most likely agree that
options: middle school students should have less homework
parents should sit with their children and help with every assignment
homework teaches children to manage their own time
young children should be given no homework at all
homework does little to raise young children's test scores
questions.explanation: Passage 1 says homework has little connection to learning for young children, and Passage 2 grants that it does not raise scores very much. They disagree about whether homework is worth giving anyway.

questions.stem: Compared with the author of Passage 1, the author of Passage 2 is more
options: concerned with the effect of homework on family evenings and sleep
doubtful that study habits matter once children reach middle school
confident that research shows homework raises young children's scores on reading and math tests
willing to defend some homework while criticizing how it is often assigned
opposed to any reading assignments for children under ten
questions.explanation: Passage 2 defends short, regular homework for the habits it builds but faults homework that is "too long and too dull." Family life is Passage 1's concern, and Passage 2 concedes the test-score point.

questions.stem:
A school is considering starting classes at 8:45 instead of 7:30 to help teenagers get more sleep.

Which of the following, if true, would most strongly support the change?
options: The school's buses already run on a tight morning schedule shared with other schools.
Many parents would need to change their work schedules if classes started later.
Students at nearby schools that moved to later start times slept more and were absent less.
Teenagers often stay up late on weekends to spend time with their friends.
Some students would rather keep the early start so that they can work after school.
questions.explanation: Evidence that later starts actually increased sleep and attendance elsewhere supports the proposal directly. The other choices are objections to the change or say nothing about its effect.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the early naturalists who proposed floods
options: accepted the glacier explanation in the early 1800s
had traced the erratics back to their parent outcrops
were the first to notice that the boulders were granite
believed that the boulders had formed in the very places where they lay
did not realize that glaciers had once covered New England
questions.explanation: Floods were proposed before ice was accepted "only in the mid-1800s," so the early naturalists did not yet understand that continental glaciers had carried the rocks. Tracing outcrops is what today's geologists do, and a flood explanation assumes the boulders were moved, not formed in place.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, "wanderers" refers to
options: naturalists who explored New England's fields
glaciers that moved slowly across the continent
boulders found far from the rock they came from
geologists who map the direction of the ice
floods that carried rocks into the valleys
questions.explanation: The "wanderers, or erratics" are the boulders that rest on bedrock unlike themselves, far from their source. The word describes rocks that seem to have traveled.

questions.stem:
To apply for a reserved parking permit, residents must submit a copy of their vehicle registration and proof of address dated within the last 60 days. Utility bills and bank statements are accepted as proof of address; cell phone bills are not. Applications without both documents will be returned.

According to the notice, which of the following would be accepted as proof of address?
options: A bank statement dated last year
A cell phone bill dated last week
A copy of the vehicle registration
A bank statement dated three weeks ago
A utility bill that is dated five months ago
questions.explanation: Proof of address must be a utility bill or bank statement dated within the last 60 days. A three-week-old bank statement qualifies; cell phone bills are excluded, the other dates are too old, and the registration is a separate required document.

questions.stem:
A vaccine trains the immune system by exposing it to a harmless version of a germ, so that the body can respond quickly if it later meets the real thing.

Which of the following is most similar to the process described?
options: A fire drill that prepares people to act quickly in a real fire
A smoke detector that sounds an alarm when a fire has started
A firefighter who inspects buildings for broken alarms
A fire truck that is stationed close to a busy neighborhood
A sprinkler system that turns on automatically when a fire starts
questions.explanation: A fire drill, like a vaccine, is a safe rehearsal that prepares a response to a later real threat. The other choices detect or respond to an actual fire rather than preparing in advance.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
options: It tells the life story of the inventor of the library card catalog.
It lists the steps a reader followed to find a book in a cabinet.
It presents a problem in libraries and then proposes several possible solutions.
It compares two competing card systems and argues that one of them was better.
It describes a system, explains what made it work and shows how its logic continued.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the card catalog, explains the standard card size that supported it and ends by noting that online catalogs kept its three access points. It proposes no solutions and compares no rival systems.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a standard card size allowed libraries to
options: lend books to readers in other cities
buy printed cards from a central supplier
file each book under three different headings
reduce the number of cards for each book
replace their wooden cabinets with screens
questions.explanation: The passage says the standard size "allowed libraries to buy ready-printed cards from a central supplier instead of writing their own." Filing under three headings was the system itself, not the result of the card size.

questions.stem:
Supporters of the new stadium promise thousands of jobs. But most of those jobs are seasonal and part-time, and studies of stadiums built in other cities have found little lasting effect on local employment. Before the council commits public money, it should ask who will really benefit.

The author's main purpose in the statement is to
options: argue that seasonal jobs are better than permanent ones
urge caution about a claim made in favor of public spending
describe the history of stadium building in other cities
praise the council for refusing to fund the new stadium
explain how a stadium creates jobs for the people of a city
questions.explanation: The author questions the jobs promise and asks the council to consider who benefits before spending public money. The council has not yet decided, so it is not being praised.

questions.stem:
In the decades after the printing press arrived in Europe, the price of books fell steadily. Scribes who had copied manuscripts by hand did not disappear at once, however. Wealthy collectors went on commissioning handwritten books for years, prizing them precisely because they were no longer the only kind.

The statement suggests that the collectors valued handwritten books in part because
options: such books had become comparatively rare and special
printed books were still too costly for them to buy
printing presses could not reproduce illustrations
printed books contained more errors than copies did
scribes had lowered their prices to stay in business
questions.explanation: The collectors prized handwritten books "precisely because they were no longer the only kind," that is, because printing had made them unusual. The statement says book prices fell, so cost was not the reason, and it says nothing about errors, scribes' prices or illustrations.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly about
options: why the glow in certain bays appears and what it depends on
how dinoflagellates are flushed out of bays and into the sea
the best months of the year for visiting Caribbean bays
why paddlers are no longer allowed into glowing bays
how mangrove trees protect bays from storms and erosion
questions.explanation: The passage explains the source of the light (dinoflagellates), the conditions that make some bays brightest and why the display is not seen every night. The other choices are details the passage does not discuss or that misstate it.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements from the passage expresses an opinion rather than a fact?
options: "Every paddle stroke leaves a trail of blue-green light."
"On a good night, though, it is easily the most beautiful sight in the Caribbean."
"The display depends on darkness, calm water and a healthy bay."
"The bays where the effect is brightest share a narrow entrance."
"The glow comes from dinoflagellates, single-celled organisms that flash when the water around them is disturbed."
questions.explanation: "The most beautiful sight" is a judgment that cannot be checked. The other statements describe the organisms, the bays and the conditions, all of which can be observed or tested.

questions.stem:
A writer argues that a city's new bike-share program has reduced car traffic downtown.

Which of the following would be most relevant to evaluating the writer's argument?
options: The names of the companies that built the bike-share stations
The price of a one-year membership in the bike-share program
The number of colors in which the shared bicycles are painted
The number of bicycle shops that operate in the city
Traffic counts on downtown streets before and after the program began
questions.explanation: The claim is about a change in car traffic, so the most relevant evidence is traffic measured before and after the program. Price, colors and shop numbers do not show whether traffic fell.

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

The results of the survey, which went to every family in the district, __was__ (A) __finally__ (B) shared __with__ (C) the school board __last__ (D) week.
options: was
finally
with
last
No error
questions.explanation: The subject is "results," which is plural, so the verb must be "were." The clause about the survey sits between the subject and the verb and does not change it.

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

__After__ (A) the storm, neither the coach nor the players __was__ (B) __able__ (C) to find the __missing__ (D) equipment.
options: After
was
able
missing
No error
questions.explanation: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "players," so it must be "were."

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

The principal __asked__ (A) Dana __and__ (B) __I__ (C) to lead the tour for __visiting__ (D) families.
options: asked
and
I
visiting
No error
questions.explanation: The pronoun is an object of "asked," so it must be "me": the principal asked Dana and me. Dropping "Dana and" makes the error easy to hear: "asked I."

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

__Although__ (A) it __was__ (B) expensive, the new printer __runs__ (C) much more __efficient__ (D) than the old one.
options: Although
was
runs
efficient
No error
questions.explanation: "Efficient" describes how the printer runs, a verb, so the adverb "efficiently" is needed.

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

__Despite__ (A) the rain, the crowd __stayed__ (B) until the __final__ (C) song __had ended__ (D).
options: Despite
stayed
final
had ended
No error
questions.explanation: The sentence is correct. "Despite" takes a noun, "stayed" is past tense, and "had ended" correctly marks an action completed before the crowd left.

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

The new __students__ (A) proved __capable to__ (B) solving the problem __that__ (C) __had puzzled__ (D) the seniors.
options: students
capable to
that
had puzzled
No error
questions.explanation: The idiom is "capable of": the students proved capable of solving the problem.

questions.stem:
Choose the best version of the underlined part of the sentence. Choice A repeats the original; choose it if the original is best.

__Walking into the classroom, the smell of fresh paint surprised the students.__
options: Walking into the classroom, the smell of fresh paint surprised the students.
Walking into the classroom, the students were surprised by the smell of fresh paint.
Walking into the classroom, fresh paint was smelled by the surprised students.
The smell of fresh paint, walking into the classroom, surprised the students.
Walking into the classroom, the students, the smell of fresh paint had surprised them.
questions.explanation: The opening phrase must describe the people who walked in. Only choice B puts "the students" right after it. In A and C the smell or the paint seems to be walking.

questions.stem:
Choose the best version of the underlined part of the sentence. Choice A repeats the original; choose it if the original is best.

The bus was late again __today, most students__ missed first period.
options: today, most students
today most students
today, which most students
today, so most students
today, being that most students
questions.explanation: Two complete sentences joined only by a comma form a comma splice. "So" adds the missing connector and shows the result. Choice B is a run-on, and C and E do not make sense.

questions.stem:
Choose the best version of the underlined part of the sentence. Choice A repeats the original; choose it if the original is best.

The new manager wants to cut costs, __improving morale, and to hire__ more staff.
options: improving morale, and to hire
improving morale, and hiring
to improve morale, and to hire
to improve morale, and hiring
improving the morale, and hiring
questions.explanation: The items in the list must share a form: to cut, to improve, to hire. Only choice C keeps all three as "to" phrases.

questions.stem:
Choose the best version of the underlined part of the sentence. Choice A repeats the original; choose it if the original is best.

Although the trail was steep, __the hikers reached the summit__ before noon.
options: the hikers reached the summit
the summit was reached by the hikers
the hikers reaching the summit
the hikers, they reached the summit
and the hikers reached the summit
questions.explanation: The original is correct and direct. B is a needless passive, C leaves a fragment, D repeats the subject, and E puts "and" after a dependent clause.

questions.stem:
Choose the best version of the underlined part of the sentence. Choice A repeats the original; choose it if the original is best.

The forecast called for __rain, however, the game__ went on as planned.
options: rain, however, the game
rain however the game
rain, however the game
rain however, the game
rain; however, the game
questions.explanation: "However" is not a conjunction, so it cannot join two sentences with commas alone. A semicolon before it and a comma after it, as in E, is correct.

questions.stem:
Which of the following is the best revision of sentence 4 (reproduced below)?

The students measured the space, researched which vegetables grow well in partial shade, and they wrote a budget.
options: The students measured the space, they researched which vegetables grow well in partial shade, and a budget.
The students measured the space, researched which vegetables grow well in partial shade, and wrote a budget.
The space was measured by the students, who researched vegetables that grow in partial shade, and a budget was written.
Measuring the space, the students researched which vegetables grow well in partial shade, and they wrote a budget.
The students measured the space and researching which vegetables grow well in partial shade and writing a budget.
questions.explanation: The three actions should be parallel: measured, researched and wrote. The other versions break the series, leave a fragment or shift into a wordy passive.

questions.stem: In context, which of the following words would best replace "liked" in sentence 5?
options: admired
noticed
tolerated
enjoyed
approved
questions.explanation: The parent association did more than like the plan: it agreed to fund it. "Approved" states that decision precisely. "Tolerated" and "noticed" are too weak, and "enjoyed" and "admired" describe feelings rather than a decision.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is least relevant to the main idea of the second paragraph and should be deleted?
options: Sentence 11
Sentence 10
Sentence 9
Sentence 6
Sentence 7
questions.explanation: The second paragraph is about how each grade uses the garden and what teachers have noticed. That the parking lot is also used for basketball has nothing to do with the garden.

questions.stem:
Which of the following is the best way to combine sentences 7 and 8 (reproduced below)?

Sixth graders track how fast different seeds sprout. Seventh graders test the soil.
options: Tracking how fast different seeds sprout, the soil is tested by seventh graders.
Sixth graders track how fast different seeds sprout, seventh graders test the soil.
Sixth graders track how fast different seeds sprout; and seventh graders test the soil.
Sixth graders track how fast different seeds sprout, and seventh graders test the soil.
Sixth graders track how fast different seeds sprout, because seventh graders test the soil.
questions.explanation: A comma and "and" join two independent clauses correctly and keep them equal, which suits the list of grades. Joining the clauses with a comma alone makes a comma splice, "because" invents a cause, the version opening with "Tracking" has a dangling modifier, and a semicolon should not be followed by "and" here.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence at the end of the passage that ties it to its main idea. Which of the following would best serve that purpose?
options: The weekend market sells tomatoes, peppers, herbs, squash and green beans.
Many schools in the region still have courtyards covered in asphalt.
What began as one class project has become part of how the whole school teaches.
Ms. Ortiz has taught science at Lincoln Middle School for nine years.
Raised beds are easier to weed than gardens planted directly in the ground.
questions.explanation: The passage traces the garden from one class project to something every grade uses, so a closing sentence about that change ties it together. The other choices add new, minor details.

questions.stem: A student is writing a paper on how sleep affects teenagers' memory. Which of the following sources is likely to be the most credible?
options: A blog post by a student who describes how she studies best late at night
A magazine quiz that asks readers to rate how rested they feel each day
A peer-reviewed journal article reporting a study by university sleep researchers
An advertisement for a mattress that claims to improve memory and focus
A social media thread in which parents share their opinions about bedtimes
questions.explanation: A peer-reviewed study by researchers has been checked by other experts and reports evidence. The others are personal opinion, commercial claims or informal self-ratings.

questions.stem:
Okafor, Lena. "Rain Gardens and Urban Runoff." *Journal of Environmental Planning*, vol. 42, no. 3, 2021, pp. 115-131.

In the citation above, *Journal of Environmental Planning* is the
options: title of the article that was written by Okafor
publisher that printed the book containing the article
database where the student found the article
name of the organization that funded the study
publication in which the article appeared
questions.explanation: In this citation style the article title appears in quotation marks and the periodical that contains it is in italics, followed by its volume, issue, year and pages.

questions.stem: A student begins researching "technology" for a ten-page paper and finds far too many sources to read. Which of the following is the most effective next step?
options: Narrow the topic to a focused question, such as how tablets affect early reading
Use only the first source in the list, because search engines rank by accuracy
Search instead for "technology and everything about how it affects society"
Read every source the search returned before deciding what the paper should be about
Choose the five longest sources, since they are likely to be the most complete
questions.explanation: A focused question makes the search manageable and the paper coherent. Reading everything is impractical, length does not signal quality, the broader search makes the problem worse, and ranking does not guarantee accuracy.

questions.stem: A student is writing about how the Erie Canal, completed in 1825, affected the economy of New York State. Which of the following would be most relevant to the paper?
options: A modern guide to hiking trails that follow the old canal route today
A list of the songs written about the canal in the 1800s and 1900s
A biography of a painter who made pictures of canal boats in the 1900s
Records of the goods shipped through New York City's port before and after 1825
A description of how canal locks were rebuilt in the twentieth century
questions.explanation: Shipping records from before and after the canal opened bear directly on its economic effect. The other sources concern art, recreation, songs or later engineering.

questions.stem: A bag holds only red and blue marbles in a ratio of 3 to 5. If the bag holds 64 marbles, how many are blue?
questions.explanation: The ratio has 3 + 5 = 8 parts, so each part is 64 / 8 = 8 marbles. Blue is 5 parts: 5 x 8 = 40.

questions.stem: A student's scores on four quizzes were 82, 90, 76 and 88. What score does the student need on the fifth quiz for the mean of all five scores to be exactly 85? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: A mean of 85 over five quizzes needs a total of 5 x 85 = 425. The first four add to 336, so the fifth must be 425 - 336 = 89.

questions.stem: If $3x - 7 = 2x + 5$, what is the value of $x$?
questions.explanation: Subtract $2x$ from both sides: $x - 7 = 5$. Add 7: $x = 12$. Check: $3(12) - 7 = 29$ and $2(12) + 5 = 29$.

questions.stem: The price of a museum membership rose from \$40 to \$50. By what percent did the price increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is \$10. Percent change is the change divided by the original amount: 10 / 40 = 0.25, or 25%. Dividing by the new price gives 20%, a common mistake.

questions.stem: What is the median of the data set 12, 7, 9, 15, 7, 10?
questions.explanation: In order the values are 7, 7, 9, 10, 12, 15. With six values, the median is the mean of the middle two: (9 + 10) / 2 = 9.5. The mode is 7 and the mean is 10.

questions.stem: What is the value of $2a^2 - 3b$ when $a = -2$ and $b = 4$?

There are 120 students in the seventh grade. Of them, $\frac{3}{4}$ take a world language, and $\frac{2}{3}$ of those students take Spanish. How many seventh graders take Spanish? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: $\frac{3}{4}$ of 120 is 90 students. $\frac{2}{3}$ of 90 is 60. Equivalently, $\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$ of 120.

questions.stem: A bag contains 4 red, 6 blue and 5 green tiles. If one tile is chosen at random, what is the probability that it is not blue?
questions.explanation: There are 15 tiles and 9 of them are not blue, so the probability is $\frac{9}{15} = \frac{3}{5}$. $\frac{2}{5}$ is the probability that the tile is blue.

questions.stem: A phone plan charges \$20 per month plus \$0.10 for each text message. Last month's bill was \$27.50. How many text messages were sent? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: The texts cost 27.50 - 20 = \$7.50. At \$0.10 each, that is 7.50 / 0.10 = 75 texts.

questions.stem: A car travels 150 miles on 6 gallons of gas. At the same rate, how many gallons will it use to travel 400 miles?
questions.explanation: The car gets 150 / 6 = 25 miles per gallon. For 400 miles it needs 400 / 25 = 16 gallons.

questions.stem:
The table shows the number of books a bookstore sold each month.

| Month | Books sold |
|---|---|
| January | 240 |
| February | 180 |
| March | 270 |
| April | 300 |

By what percent did sales increase from February to March?
questions.explanation: Sales rose by 270 - 180 = 90 books. As a percent of the February figure: 90 / 180 = 0.5, or 50%. Dividing by the March figure gives about 33%.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the solution of $5 - 2x > 11$?
questions.explanation: Subtract 5: $-2x > 6$. Dividing both sides by $-2$ reverses the inequality: $x < -3$. Check with $x = -4$: $5 + 8 = 13 > 11$.

questions.stem: In the number 3,405.27, which digit is in the tenths place?
questions.explanation: The tenths place is the first digit to the right of the decimal point, which is 2. The 7 is in the hundredths place and the 0 is in the tens place.

questions.stem: A scatterplot shows the number of hours each student in a class studied for a test (horizontal axis) and the student's score (vertical axis). The points rise from lower left to upper right and lie fairly close to a straight line. Which of the following best describes the relationship?
options: A weak negative association that only appears for high scores
A strong positive association between hours studied and score
A strong negative association between hours studied and score
No association between hours studied and score
Proof that studying one more hour raises a score by one point
questions.explanation: Points rising from lower left to upper right show a positive association, and points close to a line show a strong one. A scatterplot shows association, not the exact effect of one more hour.

questions.stem: The length of a rectangle is twice its width, and its perimeter is 36 centimeters. What is the area of the rectangle, in square centimeters?
questions.explanation: With width $w$ and length $2w$, the perimeter is $2w + 2(2w) = 6w = 36$, so $w = 6$ and the length is 12. Area is $6 \times 12 = 72$.

questions.stem: Which of the following lists the numbers in order from least to greatest?
questions.explanation: As decimals: $\frac{4}{9} \approx 0.444$ and $\frac{1}{2} = 0.5$. So the order is 0.405, 0.444, 0.46, 0.5.

questions.stem:
The two-way table shows the students in a school's ninth and tenth grades and whether each plays on a sports team.

| | Plays a sport | Does not | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Grade 9 | 45 | 75 | 120 |
| Grade 10 | 60 | 60 | 120 |
| Total | 105 | 135 | 240 |

If a ninth grader is chosen at random, what is the probability that the student plays a sport?
questions.explanation: Only ninth graders count: 45 of 120 play a sport, and $\frac{45}{120} = \frac{3}{8}$. $\frac{3}{7}$ is 45 out of all 105 players, and $\frac{3}{16}$ is 45 out of all 240 students.

questions.stem: The three angles of a triangle measure $x$, $2x$ and $3x$ degrees. What is the measure of the largest angle?
options: 180 degrees
30 degrees
60 degrees
90 degrees
120 degrees
questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees: $6x = 180$, so $x = 30$. The largest angle is $3x = 90$ degrees.

questions.stem: Which of the following numbers are prime? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: 23 and 29 have no factors other than 1 and themselves. 21 = 3 x 7, 27 = 3 x 9 and 33 = 3 x 11 are composite.

questions.stem:
A class recorded the number of pets each of 20 students owns.

| Number of pets | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Students | 5 | 7 | 4 | 3 | 1 |

Which of the following statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The median is 1 pet.
The mode is 1 pet.
The class owns 30 pets in all.
The range is 5 pets.
More than half of the students own at least 2 pets.
questions.explanation: The most common value is 1 (7 students), so the mode is 1. In order, the 10th and 11th values are both 1, so the median is 1. Only 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 students own 2 or more, the range is 4 - 0 = 4, and the total is 0 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 4 = 28 pets.

questions.stem: A box is 4 inches wide, 6 inches long and 8 inches tall. How many cubes that measure 2 inches on each side will exactly fill the box?
questions.explanation: Along each edge, 4 / 2 = 2, 6 / 2 = 3 and 8 / 2 = 4 cubes fit, so $2 \times 3 \times 4 = 24$ cubes. Check by volume: the box is 192 cubic inches and each cube is 8, and 192 / 8 = 24.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a counterexample to the statement "The sum of two prime numbers is always even"?
questions.explanation: A counterexample must satisfy the conditions (two primes) and break the conclusion (an odd sum). 2 and 3 are both prime and their sum, 5, is odd. 4 + 9 = 13 is odd, but neither 4 nor 9 is prime.

questions.stem: The weekly earnings of five part-time workers are \$200, \$220, \$230, \$240 and \$250. A sixth worker who earns \$900 joins them. How does adding the sixth worker affect the mean and the median?
options: The mean and the median both increase by the same amount.
The median increases a lot; the mean increases a little.
Neither the mean nor the median changes at all.
The mean increases a lot; the median increases a little.
The mean increases a little; the median stays the same.
questions.explanation: The mean rises from \$228 to about \$340, pulled up by the outlier. The median moves from \$230 to \$235, the average of \$230 and \$240. An extreme value affects the mean far more than the median.

questions.stem: At the same time of day, a person 6 feet tall casts a shadow 4 feet long and a tree casts a shadow 30 feet long. How tall is the tree?
options: 36 feet
180 feet
45 feet
32 feet
20 feet
questions.explanation: The person and the tree form similar triangles with their shadows, so $\frac{6}{4} = \frac{h}{30}$. Then $4h = 180$ and $h = 45$ feet.

questions.stem: A recipe uses 3 cups of milk per batch. How many complete batches can be made from 1 gallon of milk? (1 gallon = 16 cups)
questions.explanation: 16 / 3 = 5 with 1 cup left over, so only 5 complete batches can be made. Rounding 5.33 up to 6 would need 18 cups.

questions.stem: A bar graph shows a school's recycling in pounds: Week 1, 120; Week 2, 150; Week 3, 90; Week 4, 160. What was the mean amount recycled per week?
options: 520 pounds
150 pounds
120 pounds
130 pounds
135 pounds
questions.explanation: The total is 120 + 150 + 90 + 160 = 520 pounds over 4 weeks, so the mean is 520 / 4 = 130 pounds.

questions.stem: Which of the following expressions are equivalent to $2(x + 3) - x$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $2(x + 3) - x = 2x + 6 - x = x + 6$. That equals $6 + x$ and $(x + 3) + 3$. $3x + 6$ adds $x$ instead of subtracting it, and $x + 3$ forgets to distribute the 2.

questions.stem: Tickets for a school play cost \$7.50 each. What is the greatest number of tickets that can be bought with \$100? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: 100 / 7.50 = 13.33..., so 13 tickets cost \$97.50 and a 14th would bring the total to \$105, more than \$100. Round down.

questions.stem:
Last winter the Hillside neighborhood had fewer burglaries than the winter before. The neighborhood association credits the new streetlights it installed in the fall.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the association's explanation?
options: The new streetlights use less electricity than the old streetlights did.
Burglaries fell by the same amount last winter in nearby neighborhoods that got no new lights.
Residents say they feel safer walking at night under the new lights.
Most burglaries in Hillside happen in the evening after dark.
The association paid for the streetlights with money from a bake sale.
questions.explanation: If neighborhoods without new lights saw the same drop, something other than the lights probably caused it. Evening burglaries and residents' feelings fit the association's explanation rather than weakening it.

questions.stem: Which grade had the largest decrease in weekly reading minutes from 2015 to 2025?
options: Grade 6
Grade 10
Grades 4 and 10 had the same, largest decrease.
Grade 4
Grade 8
questions.explanation: The decreases are grade 4: 150 - 135 = 15, grade 6: 120 - 90 = 30, grade 8: 95 - 60 = 35 and grade 10: 70 - 55 = 15. Grade 8 fell the most.

questions.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the table?
options: Reading minutes for grade 4 students rose between 2020 and 2025.
Grade 6 students in 2025 read more than grade 4 students did in 2015.
Students in grade 10 reported reading less than half as much in 2025 as in 2015.
In each year shown, students in higher grades reported fewer reading minutes than students in lower grades.
Students read less in 2025 because they spent more time on phones.
questions.explanation: In 2015, 2020 and 2025 the minutes fall from grade 4 to grade 6 to grade 8 to grade 10. Grade 10 fell from 70 to 55, not by half, grade 4 fell, and the table gives no causes.

questions.stem:
Ticket holders for Saturday's outdoor concert should note that the event will go ahead in light rain. If the city issues a severe weather warning, the concert will be moved to Sunday at the same time, and Saturday tickets will be honored. No refunds will be given for weather.

Based on the notice, a ticket holder who cannot attend on Sunday and whose Saturday concert is moved because of a severe weather warning will most likely
options: receive a refund for the full ticket price
be given a ticket for a later season
be able to attend on Saturday anyway
receive a partial refund for the ticket
not receive a refund for the ticket
questions.explanation: The notice says the Saturday tickets will be honored on Sunday and that "no refunds will be given for weather," so a holder who cannot go on Sunday will not get money back. Nothing mentions another season or partial refunds.

questions.stem:
Most of the paintings in the exhibit are small landscapes, quiet and carefully finished. The final room, by contrast, holds three enormous canvases splashed with color, painted in the artist's last year.

The phrase "by contrast" in the statement serves to
options: introduce an example of a quiet, carefully finished landscape
explain why the artist stopped painting landscapes
show that the final room was added after the exhibit opened
mark a difference between the final room and the rest of the exhibit
suggest that the final room is the least important part
questions.explanation: "By contrast" sets the three large, bold canvases against the small, quiet landscapes that fill the rest of the exhibit.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the main point of the passage?
options: Railroads ended the lyceum movement by making it too costly for small towns to invite outside speakers.
Josiah Holbrook founded lyceums to spread the abolitionist and women's rights movements.
The lyceum began as a way for neighbors to teach one another and turned into a lecture circuit for paid celebrities.
Lyceums were most popular in frontier towns, where farmers needed lectures on soil chemistry.
Historians agree that the paid lecture circuit was a loss for small-town audiences.
questions.explanation: The passage traces the lyceum from local mutual education to a circuit of famous, paid speakers set by booking agents. Railroads changed it rather than ending it, the reform debates came later, and the last paragraph says historians disagree.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following happened as railroads spread?
options: The number of lyceums in New England fell by half.
Lyceum members began writing their own lecture programs.
Local doctors replaced visiting lecturers in most towns.
Admission to lyceum evenings became free for farmers.
Touring speakers could visit many towns in one season.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that with the railroads "touring speakers could now reach dozens of towns in a single season." Programs came to be set by booking agents, not members, and the passage gives no figures for a decline.

questions.stem: As used in the second paragraph, "handsome" most nearly means
options: generous
graceful
polite
attractive
fashionable
questions.explanation: The lecturers "were paid handsome fees," that is, large or generous fees. The meaning about appearance does not apply to money.

questions.stem: The last sentence of the passage ("Yet the original idea... mainly listened") serves primarily to
options: reject the view that small towns gained anything
introduce a new historical period after the lyceums
state what was lost in the change described earlier
explain why railroads made touring lectures possible
give an example of a famous lecturer's paid tour
questions.explanation: After listing what was gained, the passage turns with "Yet" to what was lost: ordinary people teaching one another. It does not deny the gains it has just described.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations is most similar to the change in the lyceum described in the passage?
options: A choir that sang only in one church starts performing in churches across the county.
A newspaper that printed national news begins to cover local events as well.
A school that charged tuition becomes free to every student who lives in the town.
A book club whose members took turns leading discussions starts paying famous authors to speak while members listen.
A town library that lent only printed books begins lending e-books and audiobooks as well.
questions.explanation: The lyceum moved from neighbors teaching one another to paid celebrities lecturing to an audience. A book club that shifts from members leading discussion to paying famous speakers follows the same pattern.

questions.stem:
Ana scored higher on her second practice test than on her first, so the flash cards she studied between the tests must have worked.

The conclusion depends on the assumption that
options: flash cards are the best way for anyone to study for a test
the second practice test was harder than the first one
Ana studied with flash cards for at least an hour each day
nothing other than the flash cards explains Ana's higher second score
Ana will score even higher on the real test than on the second
questions.explanation: To credit the flash cards, the speaker must assume that no other factor, such as an easier test, more sleep or other study, produced the gain. A harder second test would actually strengthen the case, but it is not required.

questions.stem:
The committee did not reject the proposal; it simply asked for more information about cost before taking a vote.

Which of the following best restates the sentence?
options: The committee asked another group to vote on the proposal instead.
The committee delayed its vote until it learned more about the cost.
The committee approved the proposal but asked the planners for a lower cost.
The committee voted on the proposal without discussing its cost.
The committee rejected the proposal because it cost too much money.
questions.explanation: "Did not reject" plus "asked for more information about cost before taking a vote" means the vote was postponed until cost details arrived. No vote, approval or rejection, has happened.

questions.skill: Main idea of a paired passage
questions.stem: The author of Passage 2 argues that
options: if the clock changes end, standard time should be kept all year
the clocks should continue to change twice each year
the 1974 experiment proved that clock changes cause no harm to anyone
sleep researchers disagree about the effects of morning light
permanent daylight saving time would help children sleep
questions.explanation: Passage 2 accepts the case against changing clocks but rejects permanent daylight saving time, concluding, "If the clocks are to stop changing, they should stay on standard time."

questions.stem: The author of Passage 2 would most likely respond to the "easy compromise" proposed at the end of Passage 1 by pointing out that it would
options: reduce the activity reported by sports leagues
force cities to move to a different time zone
require the clocks to change three times a year
keep the twice-yearly disruption of the clocks
leave many people facing dark winter mornings
questions.explanation: Passage 1's compromise is permanent daylight saving time. Passage 2 objects that it would push winter sunrise past 8:30 in many northern cities, so people would start the day in the dark.

questions.stem: The authors of both passages would most likely agree that
options: changing the clocks twice a year has real drawbacks
the 1974 experiment with clock changes was a success
bright evenings are more valuable than bright mornings
sleep researchers support permanent daylight saving time
standard time should be kept throughout the year
questions.explanation: Passage 1 says the twice-yearly disruption is what most people complain about, and Passage 2 says "the case against changing the clocks is strong." They disagree about which time to keep.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the two passages differ in their approach?
options: Passage 1 is written for sleep researchers, while Passage 2 is written for sports leagues.
Passage 1 relies on historical evidence, while Passage 2 relies on economic data from retailers.
Passage 1 stresses how people use evening light, while Passage 2 stresses the effects of dark mornings.
Passage 1 opposes ending the clock changes, while Passage 2 supports keeping the clock changes.
Passage 1 describes the 1974 experiment, while Passage 2 describes retail activity.
questions.explanation: Passage 1 builds its case on bright evenings and what people do with them; Passage 2 builds its case on morning light, sleep and dark winter mornings. The history of 1974 is in Passage 2, not Passage 1.

questions.stem:
Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter about a quarter of all known marine species. Many of those species depend on reefs for food or for places to lay eggs.

Which of the following sentences would most logically follow the statement?
options: Some fish can live in both salt water and fresh water.
As a result, damage to reefs can threaten a large share of ocean life.
Coral is an animal, although it is often mistaken for a plant.
The largest coral reef in the world lies off the northeastern coast of Australia.
Scuba diving became a popular hobby in the second half of the 1900s.
questions.explanation: The statement stresses how many species depend on a small area. The logical next point is the consequence: harm to reefs reaches far beyond their size.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred about the octopus from the passage?
options: It changes color more slowly than most other animals do.
It can see more colors than most fish are able to see.
Its eyes alone do not explain how it matches the colors around it.
It changes color only when it is hunting for food.
Its chromatophores contain the same pigment as its eyes.
questions.explanation: Because most octopuses appear to be color-blind, their eyes cannot fully account for their color matching, which is why the passage calls the question open and mentions that the skin may sense light.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, "curiously" signals that the information that follows is
options: proven by careful laboratory experiments
surprising given what came before
unimportant to the main point
taken from an earlier study
widely known among readers
questions.explanation: After describing the octopus's expert color changes, the author introduces the fact that most octopuses are color-blind with "curiously," marking it as unexpected.

questions.stem:
Bird-watchers in the valley reported far more sightings of the gray heron this year than last. Before concluding that the heron population has grown, however, consider that the valley's bird club doubled its membership over the same period, and that the club's new phone app makes reporting a sighting take seconds.

The author would most likely agree that
options: the gray heron population in the valley has certainly declined this year
the bird club's phone app produces inaccurate reports of gray heron sightings
new members of the bird club are less skilled than experienced members
bird-watchers should stop counting herons until the app is improved
more reports of herons do not by themselves show that there are more herons
questions.explanation: The author offers other explanations for the rise in reports, more watchers and easier reporting, to caution against assuming the population grew. The author does not say the population fell or that the reports are inaccurate.

questions.stem:
A city librarian argues that removing late fees will bring back patrons who stopped using the library.

Which of the following, if true, would best support the librarian's argument?
options: Many former patrons told a survey that unpaid fines were why they stopped borrowing.
Other city services also charge fees for late payments.
The library recently extended its weekend hours by two hours.
Some patrons return their books early to make room for new ones.
Late fees bring in a small share of the library's yearly budget.
questions.explanation: If former patrons say fines kept them away, removing the fines addresses the very reason they left. The other choices do not connect fees to whether patrons return.

questions.stem: According to the passage, local time was dangerous for railroads because
options: travelers on horseback crossed the tracks at unpredictable times
many trains shared tracks while following different local times
noon in western towns came several hours before noon in the east
towns refused to set their clocks by the position of the sun
Congress had not yet passed a law requiring railroad timetables
questions.explanation: The passage says railroads "ran many trains on shared tracks" while timetables listed dozens of local times, which made the differences dangerous. Noon in a western town came several minutes later, not hours earlier.

questions.stem: The author mentions "travelers on horseback" most likely to
options: suggest that railroads were less safe than horses
show why differences in local time once mattered little
explain how the first standard time zones were measured and drawn
describe the people who asked Congress for a law
illustrate how the sun moves across the sky
questions.explanation: The sentence "For travelers on horseback the difference hardly mattered" contrasts slow travel with railroads, for which the same differences were dangerous.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences expresses an opinion rather than a fact?
options: The new library cost the city about twelve million dollars to design and build.
The new library has three floors and a children's room on the ground floor.
The new library is the most welcoming public building the city has ever built.
The new library opened in March, two months later than planned.
The new library is open until 9 p.m. on weekdays.
questions.explanation: "Most welcoming" is a judgment that people could reasonably dispute. The other sentences state floors, dates, costs and hours that can be checked.

questions.stem:
Students may drop a course without penalty during the first two weeks of the semester. A course dropped in weeks three through eight will appear on the transcript with a W, which does not affect the grade point average. After week eight, students may not drop a course and will receive the grade they earn.

According to the policy, a student who drops a course in week five will
options: have a W on the transcript that lowers the grade point average
be unable to drop the course without the instructor's approval
have a W on the transcript that does not change the grade point average
have no record of the course on the transcript at all
receive the grade earned up to that point in the course
questions.explanation: Week five falls in weeks three through eight, when a dropped course appears with a W that "does not affect the grade point average." No record at all applies only to the first two weeks.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward cities that treat desire paths as "free information" is best described as
options: approving
alarmed
indifferent
mocking
bewildered
questions.explanation: The author presents these cities' reasoning favorably, noting that paving a path often costs less than repairing the lawn and describing the universities' approach without criticism.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?
options: People ignore paved walkways because they are usually placed too far from buildings.
Universities save money by never building walkways and letting students use dirt trails.
The trails people wear across grass show where walkways should go, and some planners now use them.
Paved walkways cost less to build than lawns, so planners prefer them on new campuses.
Desire paths damage lawns, so most cities fence them off to protect parks and campuses.
questions.explanation: The passage defines desire paths, contrasts cities that fence them with those that learn from them, and gives the example of universities waiting before laying walkways. It says only "some" cities fence them, and the universities do build walkways, a year later.

questions.stem:
A writer claims that a new four-day school week saved the district money, citing a 3 percent drop in spending in the first year. The writer does not mention that the district also closed one of its four buildings that same year.

The omitted fact matters most because it
options: shows that the writer misreported the 3 percent figure
proves that the four-day week cost the district more money
means that students now attend school on only three days
offers another possible reason for the drop in spending
suggests that the four-day week was popular with parents
questions.explanation: Closing a building could account for some or all of the savings, so the drop in spending does not by itself show that the four-day week saved money. The fact does not prove the opposite either.

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

The museum __announced__ (A) that __it's__ (B) new wing __will open__ (C) to visitors __next__ (D) spring.
options: announced
it's
will open
next
No error
questions.explanation: "It's" means "it is." The possessive is "its": the museum announced that its new wing will open.

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

The __judges__ (A) agreed that __Mei's__ (B) essay was more persuasive __than__ (C) __any other student__ (D).
options: judges
Mei's
than
any other student
No error
questions.explanation: The sentence compares an essay with a student. It should compare essays: "than any other student's."

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

By the time the guests __arrived__ (A), the cooks __have__ (B) already __prepared__ (C) the __entire__ (D) meal.
options: arrived
have
prepared
entire
No error
questions.explanation: An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect: the cooks had already prepared the meal by the time the guests arrived.

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

__On Fridays__ (A) the library __closes__ (B) at __six, it__ (C) reopens on Saturday __morning__ (D).
options: On Fridays
closes
six, it
morning
No error
questions.explanation: "The library closes at six" and "it reopens on Saturday morning" are complete sentences joined only by a comma. They need a period, a semicolon or "and."

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

__Each__ (A) of the three bridges __was__ (B) built by a __different__ (C) company __over__ (D) a span of forty years.
options: Each
was
different
over
No error
questions.explanation: The sentence is correct. "Each" is singular, so "was" agrees with it, and the rest is standard usage.

questions.stem:
Choose the underlined part that must be revised to make the sentence correct. If the sentence is correct as written, choose No error.

The new bus route has __less__ (A) stops than the old one, so riders __reach__ (B) downtown __more__ (C) __quickly__ (D).
options: less
reach
more
quickly
No error
questions.explanation: Stops can be counted, so the word is "fewer." "Less" is for amounts that are not counted one by one, such as less time.

questions.stem:
Choose the best version of the underlined part of the sentence. Choice A repeats the original; choose it if the original is best.

The list of supplies for the camping trip __are posted__ on the door of the gym.
options: are posted
were posted
is posted
are being posted
have been posted
questions.explanation: The subject is "list," not "supplies," so the verb must be singular: "is posted." The other choices keep a plural verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the best version of the underlined part of the sentence. Choice A repeats the original; choose it if the original is best.

__Having finished the test early, the teacher let Omar__ read quietly at his desk.
options: Having finished the test early, the teacher let Omar
Having finished the test early, it was Omar whom the teacher let
The teacher, having finished the test early, let Omar
Because Omar had finished the test early, the teacher let him
Omar having finished the test early, so the teacher let him
questions.explanation: Omar finished the test, not the teacher. Choice D names Omar in the opening clause so the meaning is clear. A and C say the teacher finished the test, and E is ungrammatical.

questions.stem:
Choose the best version of the underlined part of the sentence. Choice A repeats the original; choose it if the original is best.

Last summer she __works at a bakery and learned__ to make bread by hand.
options: works at a bakery and learned
worked at a bakery and learned
works at a bakery and learns
was working at a bakery and learns
has worked at a bakery and learning
questions.explanation: "Last summer" places both actions in the past, so both verbs should be past tense: worked and learned.

questions.stem:
Choose the best version of the underlined part of the sentence. Choice A repeats the original; choose it if the original is best.

The committee reviewed every __application, and it chose__ three finalists.
options: application, and it chose
application, it chose
application it chose
application; and it chose
application, choosing it
questions.explanation: The original joins two complete clauses with a comma and "and," which is correct. B is a comma splice, C a run-on, D misuses the semicolon and E is garbled.

questions.stem:
Choose the best version of the underlined part of the sentence. Choice A repeats the original; choose it if the original is best.

__Due to the fact that__ the road was closed, the delivery arrived a day late.
options: Due to the fact that
Owing to the fact of
In view of the fact that
Being as
Because
questions.explanation: "Because" says the same thing in one word. The other phrases are wordy or, like "being as," not standard in formal writing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best way to combine sentences 4 and 5?
options: The idea is simple, the work behind it is not.
The idea is simple, but the work behind it is not.
The idea is simple, because the work behind it is not.
The idea being simple, the work behind it is not.
The idea is simple, and so the work behind it is not.
questions.explanation: The two sentences contrast, so "but" is the right connector. Joining them with a comma alone makes a comma splice, and the others state a result or a cause that does not exist.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the passage.

A retired carpenter leads most of these classes.

The sentence would most logically be placed after
options: sentence 8
sentence 7
sentence 3
sentence 10
sentence 5
questions.explanation: "These classes" must refer back to the classes just mentioned, which first appear in sentence 7.

questions.stem:
The writer is considering adding the following sentence after sentence 9.

Honestly, buying your own tools is kind of a waste of money anyway.

Should the writer add the sentence there?
